questions.q: Who is the protagonist of "करुणा का नायक" and what is his initial attitude toward compassion?
questions.a: The protagonist is the first-person narrator (the author-surrogate). Initially, he explicitly calls compassion a "पाप" (sin) and refuses alms, arguing it perpetuates systemic dependency. A wrong answer naming the flower-seller as protagonist reveals confusion about narrative perspective – the story is framed through the narrator's consciousness, not hers.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the narrator initially refuses to give money to the beggar woman.
questions.a: The narrator refuses because he views alms-giving as a structural evil ("पाप") that destroys the recipient's self-reliance and sustains a begging economy. His refusal stems from a philosophical system, not cruelty. A wrong answer saying "he was heartless" misses his articulated systemic critique and the text's deliberate contrast between his theory and her practice.

questions.q: Using the PEEL structure, write a paragraph analyzing how the narrator's dialogue with the woman reveals his intellectual arrogance.
questions.a: Point: The narrator's dialogue displays intellectual arrogance. Evidence: He interrupts her ("मैंने कहा..."), deploys complex metaphors ("इंद्रधनुषी कोण"), and dismisses her lived experience as "अज्ञान". Explanation: His ornate vocabulary creates hierarchical distance, positioning his abstract theory above her concrete wisdom. Link: This arrogance makes his later silence a genuine epistemological surrender, not mere defeat. A weak answer would quote lines without analyzing linguistic register or power dynamics.

questions.q: Compare the narrator's view of compassion at the beginning and end of the story. What specific textual shifts mark this change?
questions.a: Beginning: Compassion = "पाप" (sin), expressed through verbose systemic critique ("करुणा... पाप है... इंद्रधनुषी कोण"). End: Silence, acceptance ("अच्छा"), witness without judgment. Three textual shifts: (1) "अच्छा" – first verbal concession, (2) Inability to counter her final challenge – intellectual surrender, (3) Final image walking away while she works – physical alignment with her reality. A wrong answer noting only "he changed" without these markers fails board marking criteria for textual evidence.

questions.q: Critique the narrator's final silence: Is it defeat, enlightenment, or something else? Defend with evidence.
questions.a: It is enlightenment, not defeat. Evidence: (1) He accepts her definition ("अच्छा") without sarcasm, (2) Internal monologue shifts to present-tense observation ("मुझे ऐसा लगता है..."), (3) Text explicitly calls her work "पुण्य कर्म" through his eyes, (4) He witnesses her continued labor without intervention – active presence replacing abstract argument. A wrong answer calling it defeat ignores the positive semantic markers ("पुण्य", "अच्छा") and the narrative's thematic validation of her view.

questions.q: Write a 4-line internal monologue for the narrator the next morning, showing how his view of beggars has changed.
questions.a: A strong answer uses first-person, present tense, echoes her "इंद्रधनुषी कोण" imagery, shows shifted perception (seeing dignity not dependency), and avoids resolving into neat morality. Example: "सुबह की धूप में उसका फूलों का टोकरा / अब पाप नहीं, इंद्रधनुष लगता है / मेरे सिक्के नहीं, मेरी चुप्पी साथ देती है / वह नहीं मांगती, मैं देना सीखता हूँ।" Poor answers retain the old "पाप" framework or lack textual anchoring.
